newsitem.title: ITALY: OPEC sees boost from growing energy demand in Med.
newsitem.headline: OPEC sees boost from growing energy demand in Med.

text.p: Given the growing demand for petroleum in the Mediterranean, the greatest potential for oil and gas exploration and development could lie in the Middle East, OPEC Secretary General Rilwanu Lukman said on Wednesday.
He said in an address to the Offshore Mediterranean Conference that oil demand in Mediterranean countries currently exceeds supply by about 2.3 million barrels per day.
The region consumes over seven million barrels of oil per day and produces only 4.7 million bpd, he said.
"Perhaps the greatest potential for oil and gas exploration and development lies very close to the Mediterranean, in the Middle East," he said.

"Here are situated six OPEC member countries which between them hold more than 653 billion barrels of proven crude oil reserves, or more than 63 percent of the world total," he added. "The OPEC members countries of the Middle East will be expected to expand their oil production capacity to meet the growth of demand in the Mediterranean and elsewhere in the years ahead."

He said the situation was similar for natural gas, with Mediterranean countries producing just over 1.7 million barrels of oil equivalent per day but consuming just under 2.4 million barrels of oil equivalent.
He said the offshore oil industry had strong prospects throughout the world, but there were a number of constraints which Mediterranean offshore prospectors and developers had to take into account.

Foremost among these was the need for stringent environment controls, he said, and at the same time there was a growth in the level of taxes imposed on petroleum products in consumer countries, "often in the name of environmental control."
Offshore exploration in the Mediterranean might well lead to the discovery of new oil reserves but these developments were unlikely to lead to a long-term surplus of oil supplies overall.
It was therefore logical that the Mediterranean countries looked further afield for their oil supplies, Lukman said.

He noted there was already strong trade with African countries and particularly with OPEC member Nigeria, and the Mediterranean can expect to increase its oil purchases from Africa as exploration and development expands on the continent.
Lukman said fresh investment capital was needed.
"In common with the explorers and developers of the offshore Mediterranean region, the OPEC member countries need economic and legislative conditions which favour this development.
"We will all benefit from a sustainable level of economic growth in the Mediterranean region and we will all benefit from the adoption of realistic legislation," he said.

He said consumers in Europe were paying some of the highest oil product taxes in the world, with the price that consumers pay for oil products being more than five times what producers earn for crude oil in some cases.
"This diminishes demand and makes it difficult to forecast future growth. The security of demand is an important issue for us as oil producing and exporting countries," he said.
